slides.title: In 1712, Sweden lived through a date no one else had.
slides.sub: It was the fix for a mistake.

slides.body:
Catholic countries had jumped to the new Gregorian calendar by deleting days. Protestant Sweden kept the old Julian one.

Its plan: skip 11 leap days, one at a time, over 40 years.

slides.kicker: It worked for one leap day.
slides.body:
In 1700, February 29 was skipped, as planned.

Then the Great Northern War got in the way. 1704 and 1708 kept their leap days, and the plan quietly stalled.

Its calendar sat one day ahead of the old system and ten days behind the new one.

In 1709, Swedes marked Easter a week before Julian countries and four weeks after Gregorian ones.

In January 1711, Charles XII wrote from his camp in Bender, in today's Moldova: go back to the old calendar.

But the day removed in 1700 had to be returned. The next leap year would need an extra one.
One day, three dates. That made 1712 a 367-day year in Sweden.

slides.kicker: Then Sweden did the simple thing.
slides.body:
In 1753, it took the new calendar in one go. February 17 was followed by March 1.

Eleven days gone overnight. Many people felt robbed of them.

slides.lead: A slow change can feel like the safe choice.
slides.accent: But halfway between two systems is the worst place to stop.

slides.line: Save this for the next half-finished change.

caption:
In 1700, Sweden tried to change calendars slowly, one leap day at a time. War stalled the plan, and twelve years later it took a February 30 to undo it.

Half a change can leave you worse off than either option. 📅

What's a change you've seen stall halfway?
